pr_title: Disable recovery monitor before recovery start
pr_body:
We do nontrivial amounts of work before we start a peer recovery, particularly recovering from the local translog up to its global checkpoint. Today the recovery monitor is running during this time, and will (repeatedly) fail the recovery if it takes more than 30 minutes to complete. With this commit we disable the recovery monitor until this local process has completed.

Closes #93542
pr_comments: Hi @DaveCTurner, I've created a changelog YAML for you.

I don't see a great way to test this change unfortunately, at least not without introducing a whole lot of other changes, and I am not even sure this feature should exist any more so I don't think it's a good use of time to build out a test suite now. I opened https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/93544 to track this debt.
I encountered a test failure that seems to have been introduced by this change so I reverted it. I'll investigate further and open another PR shortly.

issue_context.title: Peer recovery may time out during recoverLocallyUpToGlobalCheckpoint
issue_context.body: The `recoverLocallyUpToGlobalCheckpoint` step of peer recovery may take an extended period of time, but today we do not disable the recovery monitor during this step so if it takes more than 30 minutes (by default) then the recovery will time out, fail, and retry repeatedly. We should disable the recovery monitor during this step.
comments: I reverted the PR that closed this due to test failures.

review_comments: Just a question for my learning: does this mean also when the preRecovery call fails, we would disable the recovery monitor? If yes, I guess that is unnecessary but harmless since the peer recover has failed?
Closing the releasable means we _re-enable_ the monitor. But yes this doesn't really do anything, the recovery is already dead at this point.
Kind of unrelated to your change, but I find the name `failureHandler` a bit confusing. Isn't this also called when the pre-recovery step completes successfully?

Yeah I also don't 100% like this name, but nor can I think of a better one. The point is that this listener _only_ handles failures (i.e. it's a no-op on success, apart from releasing things that need releasing) and therefore needs further modification (i.e. a `.map()`) before it can be used as a proper listener.
